name: Veydan Shroud
geological_features: Layered atmospheric bands of alternating deep violet and pale gold
A stable anticyclonic storm system in the southern hemisphere with a distinctive emerald-green coloration
Metallic hydrogen layer beginning at approximately 18,000 km depth
specific_features: The Shroud — a permanent high-altitude haze of crystallized ammonia and unknown chromophores that gives the planet its distinctive violet-gold banding
Emerald Eye — a 14,000-km-wide storm whose green coloration has never been fully explained by standard atmospheric chemistry
Intense aurorae at both poles generated by an unusually powerful magnetic field
description: Veydan Shroud dominates its local system with a mass sufficient to shepherd three captured moons and a diffuse ring system of ice and silicate debris. What sets it apart from countless other gas giants is its coloring — deep bands of violet alternating with pale gold, a chromatic signature that atmospheric chemists have struggled to replicate in models. Standard hydrogen-helium gas giants do not look like this, and the unknown chromophores responsible for the violet hue remain one of the planet's enduring mysteries.

The Emerald Eye, a massive anticyclonic storm in the southern hemisphere, adds another layer of chromatic anomaly. Its vivid green stands in stark contrast to the surrounding violet bands, and spectral analysis suggests the presence of complex organic compounds that have no business existing at those temperatures and pressures. The aurorae at both poles are among the most powerful ever recorded, painting the upper atmosphere in electric blue curtains visible from neighboring worlds.

Early surveys classified Veydan Shroud as a standard gas giant and moved on, but the discovery of its unusual atmospheric chemistry drew a second wave of scientific interest. Three orbital research stations now maintain permanent watch, their instruments probing the atmosphere for clues to the chromophore mystery. The leading theory involves exotic crystal formations in the upper cloud layers, but no probe has survived deep enough to confirm this.

The planet's helium-3 reserves are substantial and commercially attractive, though the powerful magnetic field complicates atmospheric harvesting operations. Fuel companies have petitioned for extraction licenses, but the scientific community has successfully argued for protected status until the chromophore question is resolved — a delay that grows more contentious with each passing budget cycle.
